paras: The Ellis Avenue bombing was the explosion of a bomb at the property of J. C. Yarbrough, 3212-14 Ellis avenue, Chicago, at 2 a.m. on a Monday in April 1919, set off by unknown parties. No one was reported hurt, but the blast wrecked furniture in two flats and, according to the Chicago Defender, endangered the lives of six families. The Defender reported it as further evidence that "bomb throwers" were operating "unmolested" in the city.

According to the Defender, the bomb exploded at about 2 a.m. on Monday, most likely April 7, given the paper's April 12 date. The blast went off two feet from the head of the beds in the first flat of 3214, where Mrs. Joseph Davis lived, and destroyed nearly all the furniture there; her life, the paper said, "was saved only by a miracle." One piece of the bomb went down through the floor into the basement, while another blew a hole in a ceiling and wrecked the parlor furniture of Mr. and Mrs. William T. Currill.

Currill, a business associate of a dental laboratory on East 31st street, told the paper that the people in the neighborhood had always treated him with friendly courtesies. The Defender found it "strange," however, that within ten minutes of a 2 a.m. explosion "the white people who live in the community were up and fully dressed" and had come over to inspect the damage.
The coverage reports no arrests and no police investigation; the headline itself stated that the bombers remained "unmolested."

The bombing is known from a single front-page item in the Chicago Defender of April 12, 1919, printed under its own headline inside a longer article about labor and the ordering of unemployed strangers out of town. The paper did not state the residents' race or name a culprit, but it set them against "the white people who live in the community" and invited readers to draw conclusions from the neighbors' early appearance. Its emphasis fell on the danger to the families, especially Mrs. Davis, and on the bombers' freedom from punishment.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender reporter
accounts.gist: Unknown parties bombed the Yarbrough property at 2 a.m. Monday, endangering six families and wrecking furniture; the paper hinted at neighborhood complicity by noting that white neighbors were fully dressed within ten minutes.

framing.detail: The Defender headlined the item 'BOMB THROWERS STILL OPERATE UNMOLESTED', stressing the families' danger and pointing to the white neighbors' quick, fully dressed appearance as 'strange'.

record_check.dossier: The paper says only 'Monday morning at 2 o'clock'; April 7 is the Monday before the April 12 issue and is inferred, not stated.
Residents named: Mrs. Joseph Davis and Mr. and Mrs. William T. Currill (property damaged, no injuries reported); owner J. C. Yarbrough.
Not stated outright; implied Black by the contrast with 'the white people who live in the community' and the Defender's 'bomb throwers' framing.

info: Monday at 2 a.m.; the issue of Saturday, April 12, 1919 implies Monday, April 7, 1919 (inferred, not stated)
Property of J. C. Yarbrough, 3212-14 Ellis avenue, Chicago; damage in the first and second flats of 3214
Six families whose lives were 'jeopardized', including Mrs. Joseph Davis (first flat) and Mr. and Mrs. William T. Currill, whose parlor furniture was wrecked; property owner J. C. Yarbrough

sources.note: Only report: 'BOMB THROWERS STILL OPERATE UNMOLESTED', Monday 2 a.m. bombing of J. C. Yarbrough's property at 3212-14 Ellis avenue; six families endangered; white neighbors dressed within ten minutes.
